title: What's the Deal With Staring?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore why staring is considered rude and what happens when people are stared at. They cover cereal mascots that stare at kids, the human brain's categorizing and gaze-detection systems (visible whites of the eye, neurons that fire for direct gaze), and a USC study on satisfying curiosity about people with novel biological effects (women with underdeveloped arms). They discuss the psychic staring effect (scopesthesia), Edward Titchener's 1898 work, and J.E. Coover's dice-roll experiment where guesses were at chance. Further segments cover a study where staring at drivers at a stop light made them leave more slowly, a study where a psychologist staring at a person's cheek made it blush more, gaydar research on gay men and lesbians using gaze, the cooperative eye hypothesis (looking up to ask for help, following others' gaze), and the idea that being watched keeps people honest. The episode ends with a listener email from Amy, an English teacher in Malaga, Spain, and a call for listener stories about visible differences such as vitiligo.

segments.title: Opening banter and cereal mascots
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about grocery store cereal characters that stare down at kids. They cite a Cornell study finding cereal characters gaze downward about 9.6 degrees, and say the stare builds brand loyalty.

segments.title: Why staring is rude and cultural views
segments.summary: They discuss how staring is seen as rude across cultures, with Argentina noted for socially accepted male staring at women, and no culture found where outright staring is normal. They note humans constantly categorize what they see, and that things that are slightly off hold the gaze longer.
topics: why is it rude to stare

segments.title: Curiosity, novel biological effects, and the USC study
segments.summary: They discuss staring as satisfying curiosity, with examples of people with disabilities. A USC study used women with underdeveloped arms performing tasks with residual limbs; brain scans showed the brain's interest rising and then normalizing, after which people interacted more comfortably. Parents telling children not to stare is also discussed.

segments.title: Gaze detection and the eyes
segments.summary: They explain that human eyes show more white than most animals, making gaze direction easy to read. Specific neurons respond to direct gaze, and peripheral vision picks up head turns toward you. Chuck gives a driving anecdote about a woman turning to meet his gaze.

segments.title: Psychic staring effect and Titchener and Coover experiments
segments.summary: They describe the psychic staring effect (scopesthesia), the feeling of being stared at from behind. Edward Titchener's Science paper suggested it is illusory. J.E. Coover later used a dice roll to decide whether to stare for fifteen seconds, and participants guessed correctly only about half the time, close to chance. Follow-up work found no ability to detect not being stared at.

segments.title: Sponsor break: The Message podcast
segments.summary: Promotion for the GE Podcast Theater and Panoply podcast The Message, an eight-episode series.

segments.title: Staring studies: stop lights, blushing, and gaydar
segments.summary: A study where people staring at drivers at a stop light caused them to leave more slowly than a control group. A study where a psychologist stared at a person's cheek, which blushed more when they had to read or sing. Then a gaydar study on how gay men and lesbians use gaze, mixed with body language.

segments.title: Cooperative eye hypothesis and being watched
segments.summary: Staring can ask for help, as in a study where people who looked up while picking up dropped groceries got help. The cooperative eye hypothesis says people follow each other's gaze. The hosts also argue that being watched keeps people honest, such as returning shopping carts.

segments.title: Listener mail from Amy in Malaga
segments.summary: Amy, an English teacher in Malaga, Spain, writes that her students use the show to practice listening because Spanish dubbing leaves few native-speaker options. Hosts invite listener stories about visible differences such as vitiligo.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: Hosts give contact options: Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website for stories about being stared at.
